title: Open questions, kindly
hook: Sikhs discuss the Ragmala, the calendar, diet and the Dasam Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh studies: lecture halls reading Gurbani and Sikh history closely. Your line was studied everywhere.

The program is over and the langar hall is emptying. At the end of one long row, two older men are still at it over steel cups of tea. One says the gurpurab dates should follow the old moon calendar, the way his grandfather kept them. The other says a fixed solar calendar makes more sense for Sikhs scattered across the world. Neither raises his voice. A teenager comes by with the kettle and fills both cups without being asked. The argument goes on, and so does the tea. Today opens a week of questions Sikhs are still talking about, and the way they hold them.
screen: `TWO MEN, ONE TABLE, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `THE KETTLE FILLS BOTH CUPS.` → `QUESTIONS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Sikhs name several questions out loud that the panth hasn't closed. Which calendar should set the dates of the gurpurabs. Whether an initiated Sikh may eat meat. Who wrote which parts of the Dasam Granth. And the Ragmala, a list of ragas at the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, which some Sikhs recite at the close of a full reading and others leave out. On that last one, the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, doesn't pretend the matter is settled. Its readers point to a line that admits Sikhs hold differing opinions on reading the Ragmala, and then asks only that no copy of the Granth be written or printed without it. The question stays open. The book stays whole. That's a way of holding a disagreement: decide what you must, leave room where you can, and protect the thing everyone shares. On Ang 661, Guru Nanak says, here in paraphrase, that as long as we are in this world, we should listen to something and say something. Listening comes first in that line, and talk is part of a life of faith, not a failure of it. Sikhs have a word for this kind of thinking-through: vichar, reflection, turning a thing over carefully. Over the next days this path takes the questions one at a time: meat, the Dasam Granth, women among the five who serve amrit. It won't settle them. It will try to say each side the way its own people would.
screen: `QUESTIONS SIKHS NAME OUT LOUD.` · `THE CODE ADMITS THE RAGMALA DEBATE.` · `LISTEN TO SOMETHING, SAY SOMETHING.` · `VICHAR: TURNING IT OVER CAREFULLY.` · then, large: `THE BOOK STAYS WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small question people you love disagree about, and give the side you don't hold its best sentence, the one its kindest defender would say. Breathe in on that sentence and out on your own, and let both sit at the same table a while, like the two cups of tea; if you pray, rest on Waheguru while they sit there.
Open questions. The things Sikhs are still talking through, like the Ragmala and the calendar, held inside a shared faith rather than splitting it. Today's word.
Your line: questions held kindly. A disagreement can still share a table. That's today, done.

chat.says: If Sikhs still disagree about things like the Ragmala, isn't the faith just divided?
options: Not really. Sikhs hold open questions inside a shared faith: decide what they must, leave room, keep the book whole.
Yes. Each open question has split the panth into separate faiths that no longer share a Granth.
No, because Sikhs aren't allowed to discuss these questions, so nobody really disagrees.
chat.meaning: The Rehat Maryada admits differing views on the Ragmala yet keeps the Granth whole: decide what you must, leave room where you can.
